title: On the phone
job: Calls and messages — openings, closings, taking a message
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: Non c'è + . + Vuole lasciare un messaggio?

rules.text: Italy answers the phone with Pronto?, which means "ready" — it is an adjective, not a noise, and knowing that is worth more than memorising it. The identification is Sono Rohan, "I am Rohan", where English says "this is": small, fixed, and the first thing said on every call.

stare + GERUNDIO opens here, because a call is happening now: Sto parlando, Sta mangiando. L1 gave sto and stai and M2 added sta, so the auxiliary is already the learner's and only the -ando / -endo form is new. What matters is what it does NOT do: Italian uses the plain present far more than English uses its simple present, so the gerundio is only for what is genuinely in progress at this moment. Domani sto lavorando is wrong where English says "I'm working tomorrow" — M6's plain present is the repair.

This module speaks the polite third person, because you cannot see who picked up. It is also where the level's Lei ruling shows most clearly: Vuole lasciare un messaggio? has no pronoun in it at all, and that is what an Italian says. The polite object clitic La is barred from a display for the same index reason as Lei, so the frame is written without it.

Taking a message needs no new tense. Non c'è is L1-M7's c'è negated, Ha lasciato un messaggio is L1-M5's past, and Richiamo più tardi is M5's present-for-future. Reported speech — Ha detto che… — is L3's and is deliberately not reached for, which is why a message is passed on in the words it came in.

più tardi rides as one whole thing, which keeps the bare più free for M9's comparative. That is the same protection L1-M8 gave elsewhere in this collection: a common word inside a fixed phrase is not the same as the word standing alone, and the first row to claim it decides what it means for the whole course.

sbagliato does two jobs with one shape. As an adjective it means "wrong" and agrees with its noun — numero sbagliato, la strada sbagliata. As the past participle of sbagliare it follows ho: Ho sbagliato numero, "I got the number wrong". After avere the participle never moves, which is why the -o shape stands there whatever the noun beside it is.

words.note: An ordinary adjective meaning "ready", frozen into the phone greeting. Sono pronto is "I'm ready", and it is the same word.

sentences.trap: The identification is Sono, not questo è. English's "this is" points at a person; Italian simply says "I am", and a learner reaching for a demonstrative here will sound translated.
sentences.sound: PRON-to. Two syllables, the o's short, and the question is made by the voice alone.

variations.changed: just the answer, which is what a person picking up says
M5's emphatic io, which is what you say to someone who knows your voice

mistake.why: Italian says Sono: Pronto? Sono Rohan.

sentences.usage: Both ends of every call in Italy start here.
sentences.mnemonic: Pronto means ready, and Sono means I am.

words.note: The stress is on the first syllable — NU-me-ro — which English speakers usually put in the middle.
Numero sbagliato is what you say when you have called the wrong person. The gli is the soft ly of figlio.

sentences.trap: The preposition is con and not a. Italian speaks WITH a person; parlare a exists and means something closer to addressing them formally.
sentences.sound: POS-so par-LA-re kon AN-na. The double s and double n are both held.

variations.cue: Sorry, I've got the wrong number
Can I speak to your brother?
variations.changed: a relative rather than a name

mistake.why: Speaking to someone takes con: Posso parlare con Anna?

sentences.usage: Asking for someone when a third person answers.
sentences.mnemonic: You speak WITH a person in Italian.

sentences.display: Non c'è. Vuole lasciare un messaggio?
sentences.cue: She's not here. Would you like to leave a message?
sentences.literal: Not there-is. Wants to-leave a message?

words.note: Leaving a thing behind, not leaving a place — that is partire, L1-M6's verb. The sci is a soft sh: la-SHA-re.
The ggi is a long soft j, and the plural drops one i — messaggi — as M3's vecchio did.

sentences.trap: Non c'è has no subject in it. Italian says "there isn't" where English needs "he isn't" or "she isn't", and the sentence gives away nothing about who is missing.
sentences.sound: non CHE. VWO-le la-SHA-re oon mes-SAJ-jo. c'è is one syllable with an open e.

variations.display: Non c'è. Vuole richiamare più tardi?
variations.cue: She's not here. Would you like to call back later?
Would you like to leave a message?

variations.display: Non c'è. Ha lasciato un messaggio?
variations.cue: She's not here. Did she leave a message?
variations.changed: L1-M5's past, asking rather than offering

mistake.display: Lei non c'è. Vuole lasciare un messaggio?
mistake.why: No pronoun is needed or wanted: Non c'è. Vuole lasciare un messaggio?

sentences.usage: Answering a call for someone who is out.

words.note: The gerundio of L1-M4's parlare. It only ever follows stare, and together they say something is happening at this exact moment.
The same ending on an -are verb. Verbs in -ere and -ire take -endo instead: prendendo, dormendo.

sentences.trap: This form is for RIGHT NOW and nothing else. Domani sto lavorando is wrong where English cheerfully says "I'm working tomorrow" — Italian uses the plain present for anything arranged, as M6 showed.
sentences.sound: sto par-LAN-do. The stare and the gerundio run together as one breath.

variations.changed: a third person, and a different verb
the reason someone cannot come to the phone

mistake.why: Arranged things take the plain present: Domani lavoro.

sentences.usage: Saying what is going on this second — which on a phone is most of what gets said.
sentences.mnemonic: The gerundio is for now, and only now.

words.note: L1-M1's lavorare in the gerundio. All three examples in this module are -are verbs, so the -ando ending covers them all.

sentences.trap: Two verbs with no subject between them, and neither needs one. Italian drops the subject twice here, and the endings carry both halves.
sentences.sound: non PWO sta la-vo-RAN-do. può is one syllable and the accent says the vowel is open.

variations.display: Non può, sta parlando con Anna
variations.cue: He can't, he's talking to Anna

mistake.why: The gerundio needs stare: Non può, sta lavorando.

sentences.usage: Explaining why the person asked for cannot come to the phone.

words.note: chiamare with ri- on the front, which means "again" — the same prefix as in ripetere, M1's word.
One whole thing. The bare più is deliberately not opened here — it is M9's comparative word, and its first note has to be that one.

sentences.trap: Another present doing the future's work. Richiamerò exists and would sound like a promise about next month rather than about ten minutes.
sentences.sound: ree-KYA-mo pyoo TAR-dee. The chi is a hard k, and più is one syllable.

variations.cue: Would you like to call back later?

mistake.why: The present handles it: Richiamo più tardi.

sentences.usage: Closing a call you could not finish.

words.note: Shorter than momento and far more common in speech. Un attimo on its own is a complete sentence on a phone.
Invariable, because it is an adverb — È tardi, whoever is late. The adjective for a late train is in ritardo, a different phrase.

sentences.trap: attimo takes un with no apostrophe, because it is masculine and un was never uno here. M5's un'altra had one only because the feminine una loses its a.
sentences.sound: oo-NAT-tee-mo. The double t is held, and the article runs straight into the noun.

variations.changed: without please — normal, and not curt

variations.cue: It's late, I'll call back tomorrow
variations.changed: the adverb, and a different plan

mistake.why: The masculine takes no apostrophe: Un attimo, per favore.

sentences.usage: Holding someone while you fetch another person or a pen.
sentences.mnemonic: The apostrophe is only ever on the feminine.

sentences.cue: Sorry, I've got the wrong number

words.note: Numero sbagliato is what you say when you have called the wrong person. The gli is the soft ly of figlio.

sentences.trap: The participle does not agree here, because the auxiliary is ho. M10 will write down why; for now, avere means nothing on the end moves.
sentences.sound: sba-LYA-to. The sb starts the word with a buzz, and the gli is the soft ly again.

variations.changed: the adjective rather than the participle

mistake.why: The auxiliary is avere: Scusi, ho sbagliato numero.

sentences.usage: The call that goes to a stranger — and it happens to everyone.

words.note: L1-M4's verb, and on a phone it is the one that matters. With a person it takes con; with a language it takes nothing — parlo italiano.

sentences.trap: This is L1-M5's past doing the whole job. Italian has no separate way of reporting what someone said at this level, and Ha detto che… belongs to L3 — so a message is passed on in the words it arrived in.
sentences.sound: a la-SHA-to oon mes-SAJ-jo. The ha is silent at the front — the h is never sounded.

variations.cue: Would you like to speak to Anna?
variations.changed: an offer instead of a question about the past

mistake.why: With avere the participle does not agree: Ha lasciato un messaggio?

sentences.usage: Checking what happened while you were out.

words.note: Literally "until we see each other again" — and the ci on the end is M6's, doing the same "each other" job as in ci vediamo.

sentences.trap: Ciao is for people you address as tu, and on a phone you do not know who answered. Arrivederci is the safe close, exactly as Lei is the safe address.
sentences.sound: ar-ri-ve-DER-chee. Five syllables, the double r rolled slightly, and the stress late.

variations.changed: with a plan on the end

variations.cue: Thanks very much, I'll call tomorrow
variations.changed: a promise instead of a goodbye

mistake.why: On a formal call the close is arrivederci: Grazie mille, arrivederci.

sentences.usage: Ending a call with anyone you would address as Lei.
sentences.mnemonic: The ci of arrivederci is "each other".
